terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “in logic, a premise taken for granted, an assumption”. A rare word: in conversation the premise is what has been laid down, quod positum est (see assumption), or the foundation, fundāmentum.

terms.gloss: the first premise of a syllogism
terms.comment: A term of logic, paired with assūmptiō, the second premise. Outside logic prōpositiō is a setting forth, a theme or a purpose (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: the second (minor) premise of a syllogism
terms.comment: A term of logic only; in later Latin a taking up, and in the Church the Assumption.

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.23: fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs
terms.comment: Literally the foundation of a building; figuratively the ground a thing rests on (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: prōpositiō est, per quam locus is breviter expōnitur, ex quō vīs omnis oportet ēmānet ratiōcinātiōnis
phrases.english: the first premise is the statement that briefly sets out the point from which the whole force of the reasoning must flow

phrases.latin: fundāmentum autem est jūstitiae fidēs, id est dictōrum conventōrumque cōnstantia et vēritās
phrases.english: the foundation of justice is good faith, that is, keeping to what has been said and agreed, and truthfulness

sources: Lewis & Short: sumptio · Lewis & Short: propositio · Lewis & Short: assumptio · Lewis & Short: fundamentum
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
